questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the domain of \( \sin^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The graph of \( y = \sin x \) is one-one and onto only when its domain is restricted to \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), where it takes every value in \( [-1, 1] \) exactly once.

The inverse function \( \sin^{-1}x \) therefore takes exactly the values that \( \sin x \) can produce on that branch, so its domain is \( [-1, 1] \), including both endpoints.
questions.hint: Think about which \( y \)-values a sine graph can actually output — that set becomes the input set for the inverse.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the domain of \( \sin^{-1}x \) for that of \( \tan^{-1}x \) or \( \cot^{-1}x \), which really is all of \( \mathbb{R} \).
Uses an open interval and wrongly excludes the endpoints \( x = \pm1 \), where \( \sin^{-1}x \) is defined and equals \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
Restricts the domain to non-negative inputs only, ignoring that \( \sin^{-1}x \) is also defined for negative \( x \) down to \( -1 \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the domain of \( \cos^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Restricting \( y = \cos x \) to \( [0, \pi] \) makes it one-one and onto \( [-1, 1] \), which is the standard branch used to define its inverse.

So \( \cos^{-1}x \) accepts exactly the inputs \( x \in [-1, 1] \), endpoints included.
questions.hint: Cosine only ever outputs values between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \) — the inverse can only accept what the original could output.
distractor_logic: Confuses the domain of \( \cos^{-1}x \) with that of \( \tan^{-1}x \) or \( \cot^{-1}x \), which is all of \( \mathbb{R} \).
Wrongly drops the endpoints \( x = \pm1 \); \( \cos^{-1}(1) = 0 \) and \( \cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi \) are both defined.
Uses the domain that actually belongs to \( \sec^{-1}x \), not \( \cos^{-1}x \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the domain of \( \sec^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Since \( \sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \) and \( |\cos x| \le 1 \), the secant function can never produce a value strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \).

So the inverse \( \sec^{-1}x \) can only accept inputs from \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), which includes \( x = \pm1 \) themselves.
questions.hint: Secant is a reciprocal of cosine, so ask what values \( \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \) can never land on.
distractor_logic: Ignores that \( \sec x \) never takes values strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \), so those outputs (and hence those inputs for the inverse) are impossible.
Uses the domain of \( \cos^{-1}x \) instead — \( \sec^{-1}x \) has the complementary domain.
Uses open intervals and wrongly excludes \( x = \pm1 \), where \( \sec^{-1}x \) is defined and equals \( 0 \) and \( \pi \) respectively.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value range (codomain) of \( \tan^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Restricting \( y = \tan x \) to the open interval \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) gives a branch that is one-one and covers all of \( \mathbb{R} \).

Because \( \tan x \) is undefined exactly at \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \), those two endpoints can never be attained, so the range of \( \tan^{-1}x \) is open at both ends: \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \).
questions.hint: Remember that tangent shoots off to infinity as it nears \( \pm\pi/2 \) — it never actually reaches those angles.
distractor_logic: Uses the range of \( \cos^{-1}x \) instead of \( \tan^{-1}x \).
Uses closed endpoints, but \( \tan^{-1}x \) never actually reaches \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) since \( \tan\theta \) is undefined there.
Uses the range of \( \cot^{-1}x \) instead of \( \tan^{-1}x \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value range (codomain) of \( \cot^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The NCERT convention takes the principal-value branch of \( \cot x \) as the open interval \( (0, \pi) \), on which it is one-one and covers all of \( \mathbb{R} \).

Since \( \cot x \) is undefined at \( 0 \) and at \( \pi \), the range of \( \cot^{-1}x \) excludes both endpoints: \( (0, \pi) \).
questions.hint: This is the one branch where the locked convention differs from many calculators — always use \( (0, \pi) \), not \( \left(-\pi/2, \pi/2\right) \).
distractor_logic: Uses the range of \( \tan^{-1}x \) instead of \( \cot^{-1}x \); on the NCERT branch, \( \cot^{-1}x \) is instead taken over \( (0, \pi) \).
Uses closed endpoints, but \( \cot^{-1}x \) never actually reaches \( 0 \) or \( \pi \) since \( \cot\theta \) is undefined there.
Confuses the range (output values, an interval of angles) with the domain (input values, all of \( \mathbb{R} \)).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value range (codomain) of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The principal-value branch for cosecant is \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), but \( \operatorname{cosec}\,\theta \) is undefined at \( \theta = 0 \).

So the single point \( 0 \) must be removed from that interval, giving the range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \setminus \{0\} \) — while the endpoints \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) themselves remain included.
questions.hint: Cosecant is a reciprocal of sine, and sine is exactly \( 0 \) at the midpoint of this branch — that midpoint is the excluded value.
distractor_logic: Uses the range of \( \sec^{-1}x \) instead of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \).
Forgets to exclude \( 0 \); \( \operatorname{cosec}\,0 \) is undefined, so \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) can never output \( 0 \).
Uses an open interval, but \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) does attain the endpoints \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) (at \( x = \pm1 \)); only \( 0 \) is excluded from the interior.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: For a real number \( x \in \mathbb{R} \), which statement correctly describes the principal value of \( \tan^{-1}x \)?
options: It is any angle \( \theta \) satisfying \( \tan\theta = x \), since infinitely many angles share the same tangent.
It is the unique angle \( \theta \in [0, \pi] \) satisfying \( \tan\theta = x \).
It is the unique angle \( \theta \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) satisfying \( \tan\theta = x \).
It is the unique acute angle \( \theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) satisfying \( \tan\theta = x \).
questions.explanation:
\( \tan^{-1}x \) is defined as a function, so for every \( x \in \mathbb{R} \) it must return exactly one output, never a set of possible angles.

That single output is, by the locked convention, the angle lying in the open interval \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) whose tangent equals \( x \) — this is what "principal value" means.
questions.hint: A function must output exactly one value per input — "principal value" is just the name for the one angle a locked branch selects.
distractor_logic: Drops the uniqueness requirement entirely; \( \tan^{-1}x \) is a function and so must return exactly one value, not a whole family.
Uses the range that belongs to \( \cos^{-1}x \) or \( \cot^{-1}x \), not \( \tan^{-1}x \).
Restricts to acute angles only, which would make \( \tan^{-1}x \) undefined for negative \( x \); the locked branch also allows negative angles down to \( -\pi/2 \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: Which value is excluded from the principal-value range of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The range of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \setminus \{0\} \), by the locked table in Section 3.

The point \( 0 \) is removed because \( \operatorname{cosec}\,\theta \) is undefined at \( \theta = 0 \) (sine is zero there), so no input \( x \) can ever map to it.
questions.hint: Ask where the underlying trig ratio blows up (is undefined) inside that interval — that's the excluded point.
distractor_logic: Confuses this with the value excluded from the range of \( \sec^{-1}x \), which is \( \pi/2 \), not the value excluded from \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \).
\( -\pi/2 \) is actually included in the range of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) (attained at \( x = -1 \)); it is not the excluded point.
\( \pi \) does not even lie in the interval \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \) that \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is drawn from, so it was never a candidate to exclude.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Which of the following inverse trigonometric functions is odd, i.e. satisfies \( f(-x) = -f(x) \)?
questions.explanation:
A function is odd when its graph has \( 180^\circ \) rotational symmetry about the origin, i.e. \( f(-x) = -f(x) \).

Among the six inverse trigonometric functions, \( \sin^{-1}x \), \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) satisfy this odd rule, while \( \cos^{-1}x \), \( \cot^{-1}x \) and \( \sec^{-1}x \) instead follow the complement-type rule \( \pi - f(x) \).
questions.hint: Picture the graph rotated \( 180^\circ \) about the origin — does it land back on itself?
distractor_logic: \( \cos^{-1}x \) instead satisfies \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \), the complement-type rule, not the odd rule.
\( \cot^{-1}x \) instead satisfies \( \cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1}x \), the complement-type rule, not the odd rule.
\( \sec^{-1}x \) instead satisfies \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \), the complement-type rule, not the odd rule.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: The graph of \( y = \tan^{-1}x \) has horizontal asymptotes at:
questions.explanation:
As \( x \to \infty \), \( \tan^{-1}x \) approaches \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) but never reaches it; as \( x \to -\infty \), it approaches \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) but never reaches it.

These two horizontal lines, \( y = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \), are exactly the open endpoints of the range \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \), so they appear as horizontal asymptotes on the graph.
questions.hint: An open range endpoint on a graph shows up visually as a horizontal line the curve approaches but never touches.
distractor_logic: These are the horizontal asymptotes of \( y = \cot^{-1}x \), not \( y = \tan^{-1}x \).
Names asymptotes as vertical lines (\( x = \)) instead of horizontal lines (\( y = \)); the graph of \( \tan^{-1}x \) has no vertical asymptotes since it's defined for all real \( x \).
Doubles the correct bound; the range of \( \tan^{-1}x \) never reaches even \( \pm\pi/2 \), let alone \( \pm\pi \).

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: The graph of \( y = \cot^{-1}x \) has horizontal asymptotes at:
options: \( y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ only, since the graph is symmetric} \)
questions.explanation:
As \( x \to \infty \), \( \cot^{-1}x \) approaches \( 0 \) but never reaches it; as \( x \to -\infty \), it approaches \( \pi \) but never reaches it.

These correspond exactly to the two open endpoints of the range \( (0, \pi) \).
questions.hint: \( \cot^{-1}x \) is a decreasing curve — trace what height it settles toward at each end.
distractor_logic: These are the asymptotes of \( y = \tan^{-1}x \), not \( y = \cot^{-1}x \).
Names asymptotes as vertical lines (\( x = \)) instead of horizontal lines (\( y = \)).
Wrongly assumes only one asymptote is needed; the graph approaches a different bound at each end, so there are two.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: On its full domain \( [-1, 1] \), the graph of \( y = \sin^{-1}x \) is:
questions.explanation:
As \( x \) increases from \( -1 \) to \( 1 \), \( \sin^{-1}x \) rises smoothly from \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) to \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) with no dips or plateaus.

This matches the fact that \( \sin\theta \) is strictly increasing on the chosen branch \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \), so its inverse must also be strictly increasing.
questions.hint: An inverse function is increasing exactly when the original restricted function was increasing.
distractor_logic: This describes \( \cos^{-1}x \), which decreases across \( [-1,1] \); \( \sin^{-1}x \) rises the whole way.
The graph of \( \sin^{-1}x \) has no turning point on \( [-1,1] \); it moves in a single direction throughout.
A constant function couldn't be a valid inverse of \( \sin x \), since the inverse must recover a different \( \theta \) for each different \( x \).

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: On its full domain \( [-1, 1] \), the graph of \( y = \cos^{-1}x \) is:
questions.explanation:
As \( x \) increases from \( -1 \) to \( 1 \), \( \cos^{-1}x \) falls smoothly from \( \pi \) down to \( 0 \) with no dips or plateaus.

This matches the fact that \( \cos\theta \) is strictly decreasing on the chosen branch \( [0,\pi] \), so its inverse must also be strictly decreasing.
questions.hint: Cosine falls as its angle increases on \( [0,\pi] \) — its inverse inherits that same falling behaviour.
distractor_logic: This describes \( \sin^{-1}x \), which increases across \( [-1,1] \); \( \cos^{-1}x \) falls the whole way.
The graph of \( \cos^{-1}x \) has no turning point on \( [-1,1] \); it moves in a single direction throughout.
A constant function couldn't be a valid inverse of \( \cos x \), since the inverse must recover a different \( \theta \) for each different \( x \).

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: What is the \( y \)-intercept (value at \( x = 0 \)) of the graph \( y = \cos^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The \( y \)-intercept is \( \cos^{-1}(0) \), the angle in \( [0, \pi] \) whose cosine is \( 0 \).

That angle is \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so the graph crosses the \( y \)-axis at height \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) — exactly midway through its range.
questions.hint: Read the graph at \( x=0 \): it sits at the midpoint of the whole range \( [0,\pi] \).
distractor_logic: This is the \( y \)-intercept of \( \sin^{-1}x \), not \( \cos^{-1}x \).
This is the value of \( \cos^{-1}x \) at the right endpoint \( x = 1 \), not at \( x = 0 \).
This angle is not even in the range \( [0, \pi] \) of \( \cos^{-1}x \), which contains no negative numbers.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: What is the \( y \)-intercept (value at \( x = 0 \)) of the graph \( y = \cot^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The \( y \)-intercept is \( \cot^{-1}(0) \), the angle in \( (0, \pi) \) whose cotangent is \( 0 \).

That angle is \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), exactly midway between the two horizontal asymptotes \( y = 0 \) and \( y = \pi \).
questions.hint: The graph passes through the exact midpoint of its two asymptotes when \( x = 0 \).
distractor_logic: \( 0 \) is the horizontal asymptote as \( x \to \infty \), not the value at \( x = 0 \).
\( \pi \) is the horizontal asymptote as \( x \to -\infty \), not the value at \( x = 0 \).
This is the value of \( \tan^{-1}(1) \), a different function, not \( \cot^{-1}(0) \).

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Why must the domain of \( y = \sin x \) be restricted before its inverse \( \sin^{-1}x \) can be defined as a function?
options: Because \( \sin x \) is undefined for negative angles, so only positive angles can be used.
Because calculators cannot compute \( \sin^{-1}x \) unless the domain is restricted first.
Because \( \sin x \) only outputs positive values, so its inverse only needs positive inputs.

Because \( \sin x \) is periodic and many-one over all of \( \mathbb{R} \), so without a restriction, a single output value \( x \) would correspond to infinitely many angles \( \theta \), violating the one-output rule for a function.
questions.explanation:
A function has an inverse only if it is one-one (injective): each output must come from exactly one input.

Since \( \sin x \) repeats its values periodically (e.g. \( \sin(0) = \sin(\pi) = 0 \)), it is many-one over \( \mathbb{R} \). Restricting its domain to \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) makes it one-one, so a genuine inverse function can be defined.
questions.hint: Think about the vertical line test applied backwards — an inverse relation is only a function if the original was one-one.
distractor_logic: \( \sin x \) is perfectly well-defined for negative angles; that is not the reason for restricting the domain.
This confuses a computational limitation with the actual mathematical reason, which is about the function needing to be one-one before it can be inverted.
\( \sin x \) outputs both positive and negative values (its range is \( [-1,1] \)); this claim is factually wrong and irrelevant to the restriction.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the reciprocal relation between \( \sin^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The locked reciprocal identity is \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \), valid precisely when \( |x| \ge 1 \).

The domain condition is essential: it guarantees \( \dfrac1x \) lies in \( [-1,1] \), the domain of \( \sin^{-1} \), while \( x \) itself lies in the domain of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Check which variable the reciprocal is applied to, and which domain condition keeps both sides simultaneously defined.
distractor_logic: Drops the required domain condition; the relation breaks down for \( |x| < 1 \) since \( \dfrac{1}{x} \) would then lie outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s valid range in a way that no longer matches \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \).
Swaps which side carries the reciprocal; the reciprocal belongs inside the \( \sin^{-1} \) argument, applied to \( x \), not to the output.
States the domain condition backwards; the relation actually requires \( |x| \ge 1 \), not \( |x| \le 1 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the reciprocal relation between \( \cos^{-1}x \) and \( \sec^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The locked reciprocal identity is \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \sec^{-1}x \), valid precisely when \( |x| \ge 1 \), mirroring the \( \sin^{-1}/\operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \) pair.

The condition \( |x| \ge 1 \) ensures \( \dfrac1x \) stays inside \( [-1, 1] \), the domain \( \cos^{-1} \) requires.
questions.hint: This identity mirrors the sine/cosecant one exactly — same reciprocal placement, same domain condition.
distractor_logic: Uses \( x \ne 0 \) as the condition, which is too weak: values like \( x = \dfrac12 \) satisfy \( x \ne 0 \) but make \( \dfrac1x = 2 \), which lies outside \( \cos^{-1} \)'s domain \( [-1,1] \).
Swaps which side carries the reciprocal; it must be applied to \( x \) inside \( \cos^{-1} \), not to the output.
Restricts to only positive \( x \le 1 \); the true condition \( |x| \ge 1 \) also allows negative values such as \( x = -2 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the reciprocal relation between \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
The reciprocal identity here is \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \cot^{-1}x \), but unlike the sine/cosine pairs, it only holds cleanly for \( x > 0 \), since both functions have full-\( \mathbb{R} \) domains and the identity needs a sign correction for negative \( x \).

This is a distinctive feature of the tangent/cotangent reciprocal pair worth remembering separately.
questions.hint: Unlike the other two reciprocal pairs, this one needs a positivity condition rather than a magnitude condition — think about why negative \( x \) would break it.
distractor_logic: Overextends the identity to all real \( x \); unlike \( \sin^{-1}/\operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \), this particular reciprocal relation only holds for \( x > 0 \) because both \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \) are defined for every real \( x \), and the identity actually needs the extra \( +\pi \) correction for negative \( x \).
Restricts to negative \( x \) only, the opposite of the correct condition \( x > 0 \).
Swaps which side carries the reciprocal; the reciprocal belongs inside \( \tan^{-1} \), applied to \( x \), not to the output.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the negative-argument identity for \( \sin^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
\( \sin^{-1}x \) is an odd function, meaning its graph has \( 180^\circ \) rotational symmetry about the origin.

This translates directly to the identity \( \sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x \), one of the three odd-type negative-argument identities locked in Section 3 (the other two being for \( \tan^{-1} \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \)).
questions.hint: \( \sin^{-1}x \) belongs to the odd-symmetric group of three functions, not the complement-type group of the other three.
distractor_logic: This is the complement-type rule used for \( \cos^{-1}, \cot^{-1}, \sec^{-1} \), not the odd-type rule that \( \sin^{-1}x \) actually follows.
This would make \( \sin^{-1}x \) an even function, but its graph has origin symmetry, not mirror symmetry about the \( y \)-axis.
This confuses the negative-argument identity with the complementary-pair identity \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \pi/2 \), which involves a different function entirely.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the negative-argument identity for \( \cos^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
\( \cos^{-1}x \) belongs to the complement-type group, along with \( \cot^{-1}x \) and \( \sec^{-1}x \).

Its negative-argument identity is \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \), consistent with the fact that its range \( [0,\pi] \) has no negative angles for a simple sign flip to land on.
questions.hint: Since \( \cos^{-1}x \)'s whole range is non-negative, a sign-flip identity like \( -\cos^{-1}x \) could never work — think \( \pi \) minus, instead.
distractor_logic: This is the odd-type rule used for \( \sin^{-1}, \tan^{-1}, \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \); applying it here would send \( \cos^{-1}x \) outside its actual range \( [0,\pi] \) for many values of \( x \) (e.g. it would give a negative angle).
This would make \( \cos^{-1}x \) an even function, but its value genuinely changes between \( x \) and \( -x \) (e.g. \( \cos^{-1}(1) = 0 \ne \pi = \cos^{-1}(-1) \)).
This confuses the negative-argument identity with the complementary-pair identity \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \pi/2 \), which involves a different function entirely.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the complementary-pair identity relating \( \sin^{-1}x \) and \( \cos^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
For every \( x \) where both are defined, \( \sin^{-1}x \) and \( \cos^{-1}x \) add up to exactly \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \). This can be checked directly: \( \sin^{-1}(0) + \cos^{-1}(0) = 0 + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

Since both functions share the domain \( [-1, 1] \), that is exactly the domain over which this identity holds.
questions.hint: Test the identity at the easy value \( x=0 \) to quickly confirm which version of the equation is right.
distractor_logic: Doubles the correct sum; checking \( x = 0 \): \( \sin^{-1}(0) + \cos^{-1}(0) = 0 + \pi/2 = \pi/2 \), not \( \pi \).
Uses a difference instead of a sum; checking \( x=0 \) again gives \( 0 - \pi/2 = -\pi/2 \), not the stated \( \pi/2 \).
Drops the required domain condition; both functions are only simultaneously defined for \( x \in [-1,1] \), so the identity cannot extend to all of \( \mathbb{R} \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the complementary-pair identity relating \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Unlike the \( \tan^{-1}/\cot^{-1} \) reciprocal relation (which needs \( x > 0 \)), this complementary-pair SUM identity holds for every real \( x \), since both \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \) are always defined.

Checking \( x = 0 \) confirms it: \( \tan^{-1}(0) + \cot^{-1}(0) = 0 + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: This complementary-pair identity is broader than the reciprocal one — it needs no domain restriction at all, since both functions cover all of \( \mathbb{R} \).
distractor_logic: Wrongly restricts to positive \( x \); checking \( x = -1 \): \( \tan^{-1}(-1) + \cot^{-1}(-1) = -\pi/4 + 3\pi/4 = \pi/2 \), so the identity holds for negative \( x \) too.
Doubles the correct sum; checking \( x = 0 \): \( \tan^{-1}(0) + \cot^{-1}(0) = 0 + \pi/2 = \pi/2 \), not \( \pi \).
Uses multiplication instead of addition; the identity is a sum relation, not a product relation.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the complementary-pair identity relating \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
For every \( x \) where both are defined, \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) add up to exactly \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the same pattern as the sine/cosine pair.

Since both functions share the domain \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1,1) \), i.e. \( |x| \ge 1 \), that is precisely the condition attached to this identity.
questions.hint: This identity follows the exact same pattern as \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \pi/2 \) — just with the domain matching \( \sec^{-1} \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \) instead.
distractor_logic: Drops the required domain condition; both \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) are undefined for \( |x| < 1 \), so the identity cannot hold for all of \( \mathbb{R} \).
Doubles the correct sum; checking \( x=1 \): \( \sec^{-1}(1) + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(1) = 0 + \pi/2 = \pi/2 \), not \( \pi \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the sum formula for \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y \) when \( xy < 1 \)?
questions.explanation:
The locked sum formula is \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right) \), valid when \( xy < 1 \).

This comes directly from the tangent addition formula \( \tan(A+B) = \dfrac{\tan A + \tan B}{1 - \tan A \tan B} \), applied with \( A = \tan^{-1}x \) and \( B = \tan^{-1}y \).
questions.hint: This formula mirrors the ordinary tangent addition formula \( \tan(A+B) \) — sum on top, \( 1 - \) product on the bottom.
distractor_logic: This is actually the DIFFERENCE formula, not the sum formula; it uses \( x-y \) on top and \( +xy \) on the bottom, the opposite pattern.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the difference formula for \( \tan^{-1}x - \tan^{-1}y \)?
questions.explanation:
The locked difference formula is \( \tan^{-1}x - \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-y}{1+xy}\right) \).

This comes directly from the tangent subtraction formula \( \tan(A-B) = \dfrac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A \tan B} \), applied with \( A = \tan^{-1}x \) and \( B = \tan^{-1}y \).
questions.hint: This formula mirrors the ordinary tangent subtraction formula \( \tan(A-B) \) — difference on top, \( 1 + \) product on the bottom.
distractor_logic: This is actually the SUM formula, not the difference formula; it uses \( x+y \) on top and \( -xy \) on the bottom, the opposite pattern.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: When applying the sum formula for \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y \) with \( xy > 1 \) and \( x, y > 0 \), what correction must be made?
questions.explanation:
When \( xy > 1 \), the denominator \( 1 - xy \) becomes negative, which flips the base formula's output into the wrong branch relative to the true sum of the two angles.

For \( x, y > 0 \), the locked correction is to add \( \pi \) to the base result: \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right) \).
questions.hint: Both original angles are positive and each close to (but under) \( \pi/2 \), so their true sum must exceed \( \pi/2 \) — the correction pushes the raw output back up into that territory.
distractor_logic: This is the correction used when \( x, y < 0 \) instead, not when \( x, y > 0 \); using the wrong sign here would push the result into the wrong range entirely.
This is not the correction used anywhere in the locked formula; the only corrections involve a full \( \pi \), not a half.

Ignoring the correction leaves the raw formula output in the wrong branch — since \( 1 - xy \) becomes negative when \( xy > 1 \), the base \( \tan^{-1} \) result lands outside the true sum's actual location.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: When applying the sum formula for \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y \) with \( xy > 1 \) and \( x, y < 0 \), what correction must be made?

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the sine-form of the double-angle conversion formula for \( 2\tan^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Writing \( \theta = \tan^{-1}x \), the double-angle formula for sine gives \( \sin(2\theta) = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2} \).

Taking \( \sin^{-1} \) of both sides recovers \( 2\theta \) (within the valid range), giving the locked identity \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right) \).
questions.hint: This comes from expressing \( \sin(2\theta) \) purely in terms of \( \tan\theta \), using \( \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1 \) to eliminate the individual sine and cosine.
distractor_logic: Uses the denominator that belongs to the tangent-form conversion (\( 1-x^2 \)), not the sine-form, which needs \( 1+x^2 \).
Uses \( x^2 \) instead of \( 2x \) in the numerator, which does not correctly represent \( \sin(2\theta) \) in terms of \( \tan\theta = x \).
Drops the denominator entirely, which would only be correct if \( x^2 \) were always zero.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the cosine-form of the double-angle conversion formula for \( 2\tan^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Writing \( \theta = \tan^{-1}x \), the double-angle formula for cosine gives \( \cos(2\theta) = \dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2} \).

Taking \( \cos^{-1} \) of both sides recovers \( 2\theta \), giving the locked identity \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right) \).
questions.hint: This comes from expressing \( \cos(2\theta) \) purely in terms of \( \tan\theta \) — remember the numerator is \( 1 \) MINUS \( x^2 \).
distractor_logic: Flips the fraction upside down; the correct numerator/denominator pattern is \( \dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2} \), not its reciprocal.
Negates the whole fraction; this is actually the negative of the correct expression, which would give the supplementary angle instead.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the tangent-form of the double-angle conversion formula for \( 2\tan^{-1}x \)?
questions.explanation:
Writing \( \theta = \tan^{-1}x \), the double-angle formula for tangent gives \( \tan(2\theta) = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{2x}{1-x^2} \).

Taking \( \tan^{-1} \) of both sides recovers \( 2\theta \) (within the valid range), giving the locked identity \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right) \).
questions.hint: This comes from the ordinary double-angle tangent formula \( \tan(2\theta) = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta} \), written with \( x=\tan\theta \).
distractor_logic: Uses the denominator that belongs to the sine-form conversion (\( 1+x^2 \)), not the tangent-form, which needs \( 1-x^2 \).
Inverts the correct fraction; this expression is actually \( \cot(2\theta) \), not \( \tan(2\theta) \).
Squares \( x \) directly, which does not correctly represent \( \tan(2\theta) \) in terms of \( \tan\theta=x \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: The base sum formula \( \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right) \) can be used WITHOUT any correction term precisely when:
options: \( x \text{ and } y \text{ are both positive} \)
questions.explanation:
The base formula's denominator \( 1 - xy \) stays positive exactly when \( xy < 1 \), which keeps the raw \( \tan^{-1} \) output in the correct branch matching the true sum of the two angles.

Once \( xy > 1 \), the denominator flips sign and a \( \pm\pi \) correction becomes necessary, as stated in the locked formula.

Being both positive doesn't by itself guarantee no correction is needed — e.g. \( x=y=2 \) are both positive but have \( xy=4>1 \), requiring the \( +\pi \) correction.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) already lies inside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), the composite simply returns the original angle unchanged: \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

This "undoing" only works directly when the inner angle is already inside the outer function's principal-value range.
questions.hint: Check the angle against the range first — when it's already inside, no reduction step is needed at all.
distractor_logic: This is a different angle with the same sine value, but it does not lie inside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \), so it cannot be the output here.

questions.question: Evaluate \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \).

questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \).
questions.explanation: Since \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) already lies inside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \), the composite simply returns the original angle unchanged: \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)\right) \).
questions.explanation:
For any \( x \) in the domain of \( \sin^{-1} \), applying \( \sin \) directly afterward always recovers \( x \) exactly — this composite direction needs no range check at all, unlike \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) \).

So \( \sin\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)\right) = \dfrac12 \), immediately.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: For which of the following composite expressions is a range check on an intermediate ANGLE genuinely necessary before simplifying?
options: \( \sin(\sin^{-1}x), \text{ for } x \text{ in the domain of } \sin^{-1} \)
\( \cos(\cos^{-1}x), \text{ for } x \text{ in the domain of } \cos^{-1} \)

When the inverse function is applied FIRST (as in \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) \)), the result only equals \( \theta \) itself if \( \theta \) already lies inside the principal-value range; otherwise it must be reduced to the equivalent angle that does.

When the inverse function is applied SECOND (as in \( \sin(\sin^{-1}x) \)), there is nothing to check — the intermediate angle produced by \( \sin^{-1}x \) is, by definition, always already inside the correct range.
questions.hint: The order of composition matters — "trig-function of inverse" and "inverse of trig-function" behave very differently.
distractor_logic: This composite always simplifies directly to \( x \) with no range check needed, since \( x \) is already guaranteed to be a valid input to \( \sin^{-1} \).

questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin\left(\cos^{-1}(0)\right) \) by first finding the angle, then applying sine.

questions.question: Evaluate \( \cos\left(\tan^{-1}(0)\right) \) by first finding the angle, then applying cosine.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: The principal value of \( \sin^{-1}(-\dfrac{1}{2}) \) is:
questions.explanation:
By the odd-function identity, \( \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) = -\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \).

Check the range: \( -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \) lies inside \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), so it is a valid principal value.
questions.hint: Recall \( \sin\left(-\pi/6\right) = -1/2 \), and check that \( -\pi/6 \) sits inside sine's principal branch.
distractor_logic: \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \); this drops the negative sign carried over from the input.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: The principal value of \( \cos^{-1}(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}) \) is:
questions.explanation:
By the complement-type identity, \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \), so \( \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \).

This lies inside \( [0, \pi] \), confirming it is the valid principal value.
questions.hint: Unlike sine, cosine's negative-argument rule is \( \pi - \theta \), not \( -\theta \) — the range \( [0, \pi] \) has no negative angles to reach.
distractor_logic: This is \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) \); it ignores the negative sign on the input.

questions.question: The principal value of \( \tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3) \) is:
questions.explanation:
By the odd-function identity, \( \tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3) = -\tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \).

This lies inside \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \), confirming it is valid.

questions.question: The principal value of \( \cot^{-1}(-1) \) is:

On the locked branch \( (0, \pi) \), \( \cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1}x \), so \( \cot^{-1}(-1) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

This lies inside \( (0, \pi) \), confirming it is valid.

questions.question: The principal value of \( \sec^{-1}(-2) \) is:

By the complement-type identity, \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \), so \( \sec^{-1}(-2) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).

questions.question: The principal value of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-\sqrt2) \) is:

By the odd-function identity, \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-x) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \), so \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-\sqrt2) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

This lies inside \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \setminus \{0\} \), confirming it is valid.

questions.explanation:

questions.explanation:

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: As \( x \to \infty \), the graph of \( y = \tan^{-1}x \):

This is exactly the definition of a horizontal asymptote.
questions.hint: Bounded range plus strictly increasing means the curve must flatten out toward its upper bound, never crossing it.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: As \( x \to -\infty \), the graph of \( y = \cot^{-1}x \):
options: rises toward \( y = \pi \) but never actually reaches it
reaches and stays at \( y = \pi \) for all very negative \( x \)
questions.explanation:
Since \( \cot^{-1}x \) is a decreasing function of \( x \), sending \( x \) to \( -\infty \) drives the output toward the upper end of the open range \( (0, \pi) \), which is \( \pi \).

The curve approaches the horizontal line \( y = \pi \) but, since the range is open there, never actually touches it.
questions.hint: \( \cot^{-1}x \) is decreasing, so its most negative inputs push the output toward the top of its range, not the bottom.
distractor_logic: The range of \( \cot^{-1}x \) is \( (0, \pi) \), which contains no negative values at all, so \( -\pi \) is not even a possible output.
\( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) is the value at \( x = 0 \), the midpoint of the graph, not the limiting behaviour as \( x \to -\infty \).
The range \( (0, \pi) \) is open, so \( \pi \) itself is approached but never attained, no matter how negative \( x \) becomes.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: The graphs of \( y = \sin^{-1}x \) and \( y = \cos^{-1}x \) (both restricted to \( [-1,1] \)) intersect at exactly one point. What are its coordinates?
questions.explanation:
At an intersection, \( \sin^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}x \). Using \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), substituting gives \( 2\sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), meaning \( x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).

The single intersection point is therefore \( \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), and since one graph is strictly increasing while the other is strictly decreasing, this is the only crossing.
questions.hint: Set the two expressions equal and use the complementary-pair identity \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \pi/2 \) to solve for \( x \).
distractor_logic: At \( x = 0 \), \( \sin^{-1}(0) = 0 \) but \( \cos^{-1}(0) = \pi/2 \); these do not match, so the graphs don't cross here.
This point actually lies on \( y = \cos^{-1}x \) but not on \( y = \sin^{-1}x \), since \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt3/2\right) = \pi/3 \), not \( \pi/6 \).

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Which pair of functions has graphs that are mirror images of each other in the \( x \)-axis, i.e. \( g(x) = -f(x) \) for all \( x \) in the shared domain?
questions.explanation:
By definition, any function \( f(x) \) and its negative \( -f(x) \) are reflections of each other across the \( x \)-axis.

So \( y = \sin^{-1}x \) and \( y = -\sin^{-1}x \) are exact mirror images in the \( x \)-axis; none of the other listed pairs reduce to a pure sign flip of one another.
questions.hint: A mirror image in the \( x \)-axis just means every \( y \)-value flips sign while \( x \) stays fixed — look for a pair related by nothing more than that.
distractor_logic: These are related by \( \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \pi/2 \) (a vertical shift and flip combined), not a simple \( x \)-axis mirror image.
These are unrelated by a simple sign flip; \( \cot^{-1}x \ne -\tan^{-1}x \) in general (compare their different ranges, \( (0,\pi) \) versus \( (-\pi/2,\pi/2) \)).
These are related by \( \sec^{-1}x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \pi/2 \), again a shift-and-flip relation, not a pure \( x \)-axis mirror image.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: For which of the following functions does the entire graph lie in the band \( 0 \le y \le \pi \)?
questions.explanation:
The range of \( \cos^{-1}x \) is exactly \( [0, \pi] \), so every point on its graph has a \( y \)-coordinate between \( 0 \) and \( \pi \), inclusive.

None of the other three listed functions have this property, since their ranges all extend to negative \( y \)-values.
questions.hint: This is the only one of the four listed functions whose range never dips below \( 0 \).
distractor_logic: The graph of \( \sin^{-1}x \) dips below \( 0 \) (down to \( -\pi/2 \)) for negative \( x \), so it doesn't stay in this band.
The graph of \( \tan^{-1}x \) also dips below \( 0 \) (down to just above \( -\pi/2 \)) for negative \( x \).
The graph of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) dips below \( 0 \) (down to \( -\pi/2 \)) for negative \( x \), and also skips \( y=0 \) entirely.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Which function's graph consists of two separate, disconnected branches because a whole interval of \( x \)-values is excluded from its domain?
questions.explanation:
The domain of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), which removes the entire open interval \( (-1, 1) \) from the middle of the number line.

This leaves two separate pieces of the domain, \( x \le -1 \) and \( x \ge 1 \), so the graph naturally splits into two disconnected branches with a visible gap between them. The same reasoning applies to \( \sec^{-1}x \).
questions.hint: Look for the function whose domain has an entire chunk missing from the middle of the number line, not just a single excluded point.
distractor_logic: The domain of \( \sin^{-1}x \) is the single closed interval \( [-1,1] \), with no gap in the middle, so its graph is one connected curve.
The domain of \( \tan^{-1}x \) is all of \( \mathbb{R} \), with no gap at all, so its graph is one connected curve.
The domain of \( \cot^{-1}x \) is also all of \( \mathbb{R} \), with no gap at all.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Why does the graph of \( y = \cot^{-1}x \) decrease from left to right, even though \( \cot x \) is the reciprocal of \( \tan x \), whose inverse graph increases?
options: Because \( \cot^{-1}x \) is actually a typo-level error in most textbooks and should be increasing like \( \tan^{-1}x \).
Because the domain of \( \cot^{-1}x \) is restricted to negative numbers only, which reverses the direction.

Because on its own principal branch \( (0, \pi) \), the function \( \cot\theta \) itself is decreasing, so its inverse must also be decreasing — the reciprocal relationship between \( \tan\theta \) and \( \cot\theta \) does not force their inverse graphs to share the same monotonic direction.
Because reciprocal functions always have oppositely-directed inverse graphs, as a general rule.
questions.explanation:
Monotonicity of an inverse function directly mirrors the monotonicity of the original function on its chosen branch, not the reciprocal relationship between two different trig ratios.

On \( (0, \pi) \), \( \cot\theta \) steadily decreases from \( +\infty \) toward \( -\infty \), so its inverse \( \cot^{-1}x \) must also be a decreasing function of \( x \) — independent of what happens with \( \tan\theta \) on a different branch.
questions.hint: Look at how \( \cot\theta \) itself behaves on \( (0,\pi) \), not at its relationship to \( \tan\theta \), to decide the inverse's direction.
distractor_logic: This is not a textbook error; \( \cot^{-1}x \) genuinely decreases on its locked branch \( (0,\pi) \), which correctly mirrors that \( \cot\theta \) decreases on that same branch.
The domain of \( \cot^{-1}x \) is all of \( \mathbb{R} \), both positive and negative numbers, not restricted to negatives only.
This overgeneralizes; the direction of an inverse function's graph depends on the specific behaviour of the original function on its chosen branch, not on a blanket rule about reciprocals.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the graph of \( y = \sec^{-1}x \) for \( x \le -1 \)?
options: It lies entirely in the lower half of the range, with \( y \) values between \( 0 \) and \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
It crosses through \( y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) at some point on this branch.
It is a mirror image of the \( x \ge 1 \) branch reflected in the \( x \)-axis.
It lies entirely in the upper half of the range, with \( y \) values between \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) and \( \pi \).
questions.explanation:
For \( x \ge 1 \), \( \sec^{-1}x \) rises from \( 0 \) (at \( x=1 \)) toward, but never reaching, \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

By the identity \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \), the branch for \( x \le -1 \) is the complement of this: it runs from just above \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) (as \( x \to -\infty \)) up to \( \pi \) (at \( x=-1 \)), placing it entirely in the upper half \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \).
questions.hint: Use \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \) to relate the left branch's height back to the already-known right branch.
distractor_logic: That description fits the \( x \ge 1 \) branch instead, where \( \sec^{-1}x \) ranges from \( 0 \) up to (but not including) \( \pi/2 \).
The graph never crosses \( y = \pi/2 \) at all, on either branch — that value is explicitly excluded from the range of \( \sec^{-1}x \).
The two branches are related by \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \), a point-symmetry about \( (0, \pi/2) \), not a reflection in the \( x \)-axis.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Using the reciprocal identity, express \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) in terms of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \).
questions.explanation:
The identity \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) requires matching \( \dfrac1x = \dfrac12 \), which gives \( x = 2 \).

Since \( |2| \ge 1 \), the domain condition holds, so \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) \) — and indeed both sides equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Set \( 1/x \) equal to the given fraction and solve for \( x \) — that \( x \) becomes the argument of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \).
distractor_logic: Keeps the reciprocal instead of undoing it; since the identity is \( \sin^{-1}(1/x) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \), matching \( 1/x = 1/2 \) gives \( x = 2 \), not \( x = 1/2 \).
Introduces a spurious negative sign; the original expression \( \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right) \) is positive, so its equivalent \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \) form must be too.
Flips the sign of \( x \) itself; this would correspond to \( \sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right) \), not \( \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right) \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Using the reciprocal identity, express \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) \) in terms of \( \sec^{-1} \).
questions.explanation:
The identity \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \sec^{-1}x \) requires matching \( \dfrac1x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \), which gives \( x = \sqrt2 \).

Since \( |\sqrt2| \ge 1 \), the domain condition holds, so \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) = \sec^{-1}(\sqrt2) \) — and indeed both sides equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Set \( 1/x \) equal to the given value and solve for \( x \) — that becomes the argument of \( \sec^{-1} \).
distractor_logic: Keeps the reciprocal instead of undoing it; matching \( 1/x = 1/\sqrt2 \) gives \( x = \sqrt2 \), not \( x = 1/\sqrt2 \).
Introduces a spurious negative sign; the original expression is positive, so its \( \sec^{-1} \) equivalent must be too.
Flips the sign of \( x \) itself; this would correspond to \( \cos^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) \), not \( \cos^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Using the reciprocal identity (valid for \( x > 0 \)), express \( \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) \) in terms of \( \cot^{-1} \).
questions.explanation:
The identity \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \cot^{-1}x \) (for \( x>0 \)) requires matching \( \dfrac1x = \sqrt3 \), which gives \( x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \).

Since \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} > 0 \), the domain condition holds, so \( \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) = \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \) — and indeed both sides equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Set \( 1/x \) equal to \( \sqrt3 \) and solve for \( x \) — remember the result must stay positive here.
distractor_logic: Keeps the reciprocal instead of undoing it; matching \( 1/x = \sqrt3 \) gives \( x = 1/\sqrt3 \), not \( x = \sqrt3 \).
Introduces a spurious negative sign; the original expression is positive, so its \( \cot^{-1} \) equivalent must be too.
Flips the sign of \( x \) itself; this would correspond to \( \tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3) \), not \( \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: If \( \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), find \( \cos^{-1}(-x) \) using the negative-argument identity.
questions.explanation:
The negative-argument identity gives \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \).

Substituting \( \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), this becomes \( \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Substitute the given angle directly into \( \pi - \cos^{-1}x \) — no need to know \( x \) itself.
distractor_logic: Wrongly applies the odd-type rule (\( -\theta \)) to \( \cos^{-1} \), which actually follows the complement-type rule \( \pi - \theta \); also, this negative angle isn't even in \( \cos^{-1} \)'s range \( [0,\pi] \).
Leaves the value unchanged, as if \( \cos^{-1}x \) were an even function; but \( \cos^{-1}(-x) \ne \cos^{-1}x \) in general.
Uses \( \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) instead of \( \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), mixing up the given angle with an unrelated one.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: If \( \sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \), find \( \sin^{-1}(-x) \) using the negative-argument identity.
questions.explanation:
The negative-argument identity gives \( \sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x \), since \( \sin^{-1} \) is an odd function.

Substituting \( \sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \), this becomes \( -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Sine's inverse is odd — the negative-argument identity is just a straightforward sign flip here.
distractor_logic: Leaves the value unchanged, as if \( \sin^{-1}x \) were an even function; but \( \sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x \), which changes the sign.
Wrongly applies the complement-type rule \( \pi - \theta \), which belongs to \( \cos^{-1}, \cot^{-1}, \sec^{-1} \), not \( \sin^{-1} \).
Combines both errors above: applies \( \pi - \theta \) and then negates unnecessarily.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: If \( \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), find \( \cot^{-1}x \) using the complementary-pair identity.
questions.explanation:
The complementary-pair identity gives \( \tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \cot^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1}x \).

Substituting \( \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \), this becomes \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Rearrange \( \tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \pi/2 \) to isolate \( \cot^{-1}x \), then substitute the given value.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \pi - \theta \) (the negative-argument rule) instead of \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta \) (the complementary-pair rule); these are two different identities.
Wrongly negates the given angle, which isn't what the complementary-pair identity does at all.
Leaves the value unchanged, ignoring that \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \) are generally different values for the same \( x \).

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: If \( \sec^{-1}x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \), find \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) using the complementary-pair identity.
questions.explanation:
The complementary-pair identity gives \( \sec^{-1}x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sec^{-1}x \).

Substituting \( \sec^{-1}x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \), this becomes \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \), which correctly lies inside \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \).
questions.hint: Don't assume the answer must be positive — subtracting a large angle from \( \pi/2 \) can legitimately give a negative result.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign that results from subtracting a value larger than \( \pi/2 \); \( \pi/2 - 2\pi/3 \) is genuinely negative.
Adds instead of subtracting; the complementary-pair identity requires \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \pi/2 - \sec^{-1}x \), not \( \pi/2 + \sec^{-1}x \).
This angle lies outside the range \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \) of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) entirely, so it could never be valid regardless of the arithmetic.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: For which of the following values of \( x \) does the identity \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) actually apply?
questions.explanation:
The identity \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) requires \( |x| \ge 1 \), so that \( \dfrac1x \) lands inside \( [-1,1] \), the domain of \( \sin^{-1} \).

Among the choices, only \( x = -2 \) satisfies \( |x| \ge 1 \); the other three all lie strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \), where the identity simply doesn't apply.
questions.hint: Check each option against \( |x| \ge 1 \) directly before worrying about the value of the expression itself.
distractor_logic: This fails the required condition \( |x| \ge 1 \), since \( \left|\tfrac12\right| = \tfrac12 < 1 \); indeed \( 1/x = 2 \), which is outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s domain, so the left side isn't even defined.
Also fails \( |x| \ge 1 \), since \( 0.8 < 1 \); here \( 1/x = 1.25 \), again outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s domain.
Also fails \( |x| \ge 1 \), since \( \left|-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right| \approx 0.707 < 1 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) \) using the sum formula.
questions.explanation:
Here \( xy = \dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac13 = \dfrac16 < 1 \), so the base formula applies directly without correction.

\( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac12\cdot\frac13}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5/6}{5/6}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Check \( xy \) against \( 1 \) first — here it's comfortably below, so the base formula alone will do.
distractor_logic: This is not what the formula produces here; carrying out the computation gives exactly \( \pi/4 \), not \( \pi/3 \).

Stops halfway through; \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{5/6}{5/6}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) \) should be simplified all the way to \( \pi/4 \), a standard angle, not left as an unsimplified fraction inside the inverse tangent.
This angle would require the sum to exceed \( \pi/2 \), which is far too large for the sum of two small positive angles like \( \tan^{-1}(1/2) \) and \( \tan^{-1}(1/3) \), each under \( \pi/4 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3) \) using the sum formula with the appropriate correction.
questions.explanation:
Here \( xy = 6 > 1 \) and both \( x, y > 0 \), so the \( +\pi \) correction is required.

The raw formula gives \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2+3}{1-6}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{-5}\right) = \tan^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Adding the correction: \( \pi + \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: First check the correction condition (\( xy>1 \), both positive means add \( \pi \)), then compute the raw formula and add \( \pi \) to it.
distractor_logic: This is the raw, uncorrected base-formula output — \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{5}{-5}\right)=\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\pi/4 \); since \( xy=6>1 \) and both \( x,y>0 \), the required \( +\pi \) correction was never applied.
Drops the correction's effect entirely while also losing the negative sign the raw formula actually produces; neither matches the true sum.
Applies the correction with the wrong sign, effectively adding \( 2\pi \) worth of adjustment instead of the required single \( +\pi \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(3) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) using the difference formula.
questions.explanation:
The difference formula gives \( \tan^{-1}(3) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3-\frac12}{1+3\cdot\frac12}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5/2}{5/2}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

Notice that neither \( \tan^{-1}(3) \) nor \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right) \) is individually a standard angle — the formula is essential here, not optional.
questions.hint: Substitute directly into \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-y}{1+xy}\right) \) with \( x=3, y=1/2 \), then simplify the resulting fraction fully.
distractor_logic: This does not match the formula's actual output here; the computation simplifies exactly to \( \pi/4 \), not \( \pi/6 \).
Stops halfway through; \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{5/2}{5/2}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) \) should be simplified all the way to the standard angle \( \pi/4 \), not left as an unsimplified fraction.
This is not a value produced by the formula at all here — the actual result reduces to exactly \( \pi/4 \), one of the six standard \( \pi \)-fraction angles, not \( 5\pi/12 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(2) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) \) using the difference formula.
questions.explanation: The difference formula gives \( \tan^{-1}(2) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2-\frac13}{1+2\cdot\frac13}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5/3}{5/3}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Substitute directly into \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-y}{1+xy}\right) \) with \( x=2, y=1/3 \), then simplify the resulting fraction fully.
distractor_logic: This does not match the formula's actual output here; the computation simplifies exactly to \( \pi/4 \), not \( \pi/3 \).
Stops halfway through; \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{5/3}{5/3}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) \) should be simplified all the way to the standard angle \( \pi/4 \).
Gets the sign wrong; since \( \tan^{-1}(2) > \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac13\right) \), the difference must be positive, not negative.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Using the sine-form double-angle conversion, express \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \) as a single evaluated angle.
questions.explanation:
With \( x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \), the sine-form gives \( 2x/(1+x^2) = \dfrac{2/\sqrt3}{1+1/3} = \dfrac{2/\sqrt3}{4/3} = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \).

So \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) — matching the direct check that \( \tan^{-1}\left(1/\sqrt3\right) = \pi/6 \), so double that is indeed \( \pi/3 \).
questions.hint: Compute \( \dfrac{2x}{1+x^2} \) first, then recognize the resulting fraction as a standard sine value.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \( \tan^{-1}\left(1/\sqrt3\right) \) itself, not its double; the whole point of the formula is to find TWICE that angle.
Leaves the expression in an intermediate, unconverted form instead of actually applying the sine-form conversion formula as asked.
Doubles the correct answer again; \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(1/\sqrt3\right) \) is twice \( \pi/6 \), which is \( \pi/3 \), not twice \( \pi/3 \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Using the cosine-form double-angle conversion, express \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) \) as a single evaluated angle.
options: \( \cos^{-1}(0)... \text{ left unsimplified, an incomplete final answer} \)
questions.explanation:
With \( x = 1 \), the cosine-form gives \( (1-x^2)/(1+x^2) = 0/2 = 0 \).

So \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) = \cos^{-1}(0) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) — matching the direct check that \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \pi/4 \), so double that is indeed \( \pi/2 \).
questions.hint: Compute \( \dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2} \) first, then evaluate the resulting \( \cos^{-1} \) all the way to a standard angle.
distractor_logic: This is \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) itself, not its double; the formula is meant to find twice this angle.
Correctly reaches the intermediate expression \( \cos^{-1}(0) \) but fails to complete the evaluation to its standard value \( \pi/2 \), which the question explicitly asks for.
This is the value of \( \dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2} \) itself (the argument fed into \( \cos^{-1} \)), not the final angle produced by taking \( \cos^{-1} \) of it.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Using the tangent-form double-angle conversion, express \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \) as a single evaluated angle.
questions.explanation:
With \( x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \), the tangent-form gives \( \dfrac{2x}{1-x^2} = \dfrac{2/\sqrt3}{1-1/3} = \dfrac{2/\sqrt3}{2/3} = \sqrt3 \).

Since \( x = 1/\sqrt3 \) satisfies \( -1 < x < 1 \), the tangent-form applies directly here: \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Always check \( -1 < x < 1 \) before using this particular form — here it holds, so proceed directly.
distractor_logic: This is \( \tan^{-1}\left(1/\sqrt3\right) \) itself, not its double.
Correctly reaches the intermediate expression \( \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) \) but fails to complete the evaluation to its standard value \( \pi/3 \), which the question explicitly asks for.
