questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Using the sine-form double-angle conversion, express \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) \) as a single evaluated angle.
questions.explanation:
With \( x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \), the sine-form gives \( 2x/(1+x^2) = \dfrac{-2/\sqrt3}{4/3} = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \).

So \( 2\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \), matching the direct check that \( \tan^{-1}\left(-1/\sqrt3\right) = -\pi/6 \), doubled.
questions.hint: Keep track of the sign throughout — a negative \( x \) here should carry all the way to a negative final angle.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; since the original angle \( \tan^{-1}\left(-1/\sqrt3\right) \) is negative, its double must be negative too.
This is the value of \( \tan^{-1}\left(-1/\sqrt3\right) \) itself, not its double.
Correctly identifies the sine-form's argument only up to its magnitude but drops the negative sign that should carry through from \( x=-1/\sqrt3 \), and also leaves the expression unevaluated.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) lies outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), it must first be replaced by an in-range angle with the same sine.

Using \( \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\pi - \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \), and since \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) IS inside the range, \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Since the given angle is outside the range, use \( \sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\theta \) to find an equal-sine angle that IS inside the range.
distractor_logic: Assumes \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta \) always holds; but \( 2\pi/3 \) lies outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \), so this shortcut fails here.
Gets the reduced angle's sign wrong; the correct in-range equivalent angle is positive \( \pi/3 \), not negative.
This is the value of \( \sin\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \) itself (a ratio), not the final angle the composite evaluates to.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \) lies outside \( \cos^{-1} \)'s range \( [0, \pi] \), it must be replaced by an in-range angle with the same cosine.

Using the fact that cosine is even and \( 2\pi \)-periodic, \( \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(2\pi - \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \), and \( \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) IS inside \( [0,\pi] \), so \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: For an angle beyond \( \pi \), use \( \cos(2\pi - \theta) = \cos\theta \) to find an equal-cosine angle inside \( [0,\pi] \).
distractor_logic: Assumes \( \cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)=\theta \) always holds; but \( 4\pi/3 \) lies outside \( \cos^{-1} \)'s range \( [0,\pi] \), so this shortcut fails here.
This angle isn't even in the range \( [0,\pi] \) of \( \cos^{-1}x \), which contains no negative numbers at all.
Uses the wrong reduction; \( \cos\left(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) \) does not equal \( \cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \) (they have opposite signs), so this is not the correct equivalent angle.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) lies outside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \), it must be replaced by an in-range angle with the same tangent.

Using the \( \pi \)-periodicity of tangent, \( \tan\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \tan\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \pi\right) = \tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \), and \( -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \) IS inside the range, so \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Tangent repeats every \( \pi \), not \( 2\pi \) — subtract \( \pi \) from the given angle to land inside the range.
distractor_logic: Assumes \( \tan^{-1}(\tan\theta)=\theta \) always holds; but \( 2\pi/3 \) lies outside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range \( \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \), so this shortcut fails here.
Gets the sign of the reduced angle wrong; the correct in-range equivalent has a negative sign, not positive.
Confuses the final angle with the actual numeric value of \( \tan\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \), which is a ratio, not the angle the composite should evaluate to.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin\left(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac35\right)\right) \) using the Pythagorean relation between sine and cosine.
questions.explanation:
Let \( \theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac35\right) \), so \( \cos\theta = \dfrac35 \). Since \( \theta \in [0,\pi] \) and \( \cos\theta > 0 \), \( \theta \) lies in the first quadrant, where \( \sin\theta \ge 0 \).

Using \( \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 \): \( \sin\theta = \sqrt{1-\left(\tfrac35\right)^2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{16}{25}} = \dfrac45 \) (matching the familiar 3-4-5 right triangle).
questions.hint: Picture a right triangle with adjacent side \( 3 \) and hypotenuse \( 5 \) — the opposite side (and hence \( \sin\theta \)) is then \( 4 \).
distractor_logic: This is the given value of \( \cos\theta \) itself, not \( \sin\theta \) for the same angle.
Introduces a spurious negative sign; since \( \cos^{-1}\left(\tfrac35\right) \) lies in \( [0,\pi] \) with a positive cosine, the angle is in the first quadrant, where sine is also positive.
This is the ratio \( \tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta \), not \( \sin\theta \) itself.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac35\right)\right) \) using the Pythagorean relation.
questions.explanation:
Let \( \theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac35\right) \), so \( \sin\theta = \dfrac35 \). Since \( \theta \in \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \) and \( \sin\theta > 0 \), \( \theta \) lies in the first quadrant, where \( \cos\theta \ge 0 \).

Using \( \cos\theta = \sqrt{1-\left(\tfrac35\right)^2} = \dfrac45 \), we get \( \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{3/5}{4/5} = \dfrac34 \).
questions.hint: Same 3-4-5 triangle idea as before, but now take the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side.
distractor_logic: This is the given value of \( \sin\theta \) itself, not \( \tan\theta \) for the same angle.
Inverts the correct ratio; \( \tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta = (3/5)/(4/5) = 3/4 \), not its reciprocal.

Introduces a spurious negative sign; since \( \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac35\right) \) lies in \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \) with a positive sine, the angle is in the first quadrant, where cosine (and hence tangent) is also positive.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \cos\left(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac43\right)\right) \) using the Pythagorean relation.
questions.explanation:
Let \( \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac43\right) \), so \( \tan\theta = \dfrac43 \), which corresponds to a right triangle with opposite side \( 4 \), adjacent side \( 3 \), and hypotenuse \( 5 \) (the familiar 3-4-5 triangle).

Since \( \theta \in \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \) and \( \tan\theta > 0 \), \( \theta \) is in the first quadrant, so \( \cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac35 \).
questions.hint: Build the 3-4-5 triangle from the given tangent ratio, then read off cosine as adjacent over hypotenuse.
distractor_logic: This is the sine of the same angle, not its cosine; the two are swapped here.
This is the given value of \( \tan\theta \) itself, not \( \cos\theta \) for the same angle.

Introduces a spurious negative sign; since \( \tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac43\right) \) lies in \( \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \) with a positive tangent, the angle is in the first quadrant, where cosine is also positive.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \sin\left(\tan^{-1}(1)\right) \).
questions.explanation:
\( \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), a standard angle, so \( \sin\left(\tan^{-1}(1)\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).

This can also be confirmed via the Pythagorean relation: \( \tan\theta = 1 \) corresponds to a right triangle with both legs equal, giving \( \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).
questions.hint: Since \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) happens to be a standard angle here, you can evaluate it directly rather than building a triangle.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \( \tan\theta \) itself (the given ratio), not \( \sin\theta \) for the same angle.
This is the intermediate angle \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) itself, not the final value after applying \( \sin \) to it.
This is the sine of a different standard angle (\( \pi/3 \)), not of \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \pi/4 \).

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: Evaluate \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) \).
questions.explanation:
Since \( -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \) lies outside \( \cos^{-1} \)'s range \( [0, \pi] \), it must be replaced by an in-range angle with the same cosine.

Since cosine is an even function, \( \cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \), and \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) IS inside \( [0,\pi] \), so \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Cosine is even, so a negative angle can always be replaced by its positive counterpart before checking the range.
distractor_logic: Assumes \( \cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)=\theta \) always holds; but \( -\pi/3 \) lies outside \( \cos^{-1} \)'s range \( [0,\pi] \) (which contains no negative angles at all), so this shortcut fails here.
Uses the wrong reduction; \( \cos\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \) does not equal \( \cos\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \) (they have opposite signs).
This is a different standard angle entirely, not connected to any step in evaluating \( \cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What can be said about \( \sin^{-1}(2) \)?
options: It is not defined, since \( 2 \) does not lie in the domain \( [-1, 1] \) of \( \sin^{-1}x \).
It equals \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the largest value \( \sin^{-1}x \) can output.
It equals \( 2 \) radians directly, since inverse trig functions return the input angle.
It is not defined, since \( 2 \) is larger than \( \pi \), the largest possible angle.
questions.explanation:
\( \sin^{-1}x \) is defined only for \( x \in [-1, 1] \), since \( \sin\theta \) itself never exceeds \( 1 \) or goes below \( -1 \) for any real \( \theta \).

Because \( 2 \) lies outside \( [-1, 1] \), \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) is simply not defined — there is no angle whose sine equals \( 2 \).
questions.hint: Always check the input against the domain first; sine itself never produces a value bigger than \( 1 \).
distractor_logic: Confuses \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the largest OUTPUT of \( \sin^{-1}x \), with a valid response for an input outside the domain — an out-of-domain input has no output at all, largest or otherwise.
Confuses inverse trigonometric functions with identity functions; \( \sin^{-1}x \) does not simply return \( x \).
Gives the right conclusion (undefined) for the wrong reason: the issue is that \( 2 \) falls outside the domain \( [-1,1] \), not a comparison with \( \pi \), which is irrelevant to the input side.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What can be said about \( \sec^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \)?
options: It is not defined, since \( \dfrac12 \) lies inside \( (-1, 1) \), which is excluded from the domain of \( \sec^{-1}x \).
It equals \( 2 \), using the reciprocal relation without checking any domain condition.
It is defined and equals \( 0 \), since \( \sec^{-1}x \) is defined for all real \( x \).
questions.explanation:
The domain of \( \sec^{-1}x \) is \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), because \( \sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \) can never take a value strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \).

Since \( \dfrac12 \) lies inside the excluded interval \( (-1, 1) \), \( \sec^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) is simply not defined.
questions.hint: Don't confuse this with \( \cos^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right) \), which IS defined — \( \sec^{-1} \) and \( \cos^{-1} \) have different domains.
distractor_logic: Wrongly treats \( \sec^{-1}x \) as interchangeable with \( \cos^{-1}x \); the two functions have different domains, and this input is invalid for \( \sec^{-1} \) even though it's valid for \( \cos^{-1} \).
Confuses the reciprocal of the INPUT (which would need its own domain check) with the actual output angle, and skips checking whether the relation even applies here.
Incorrectly claims \( \sec^{-1}x \) is defined on all of \( \mathbb{R} \); its domain is \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), which excludes \( \dfrac12 \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value of \( \cot^{-1}(0) \)?
questions.explanation:
On the locked branch \( (0, \pi) \), the angle whose cotangent is \( 0 \) is \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), since \( \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 \).

This is a common trap because some non-NCERT references use a different principal branch for \( \cot^{-1} \) that would give \( 0 \) instead — always use the locked range \( (0, \pi) \) here.
questions.hint: This is the single most common branch-convention trap for \( \cot^{-1} \) — always check against the locked range \( (0,\pi) \), not a calculator default.
distractor_logic: This is the value some calculators or foreign textbooks give using a different range convention for \( \cot^{-1} \); on the NCERT branch \( (0, \pi) \), \( \cot^{-1}(0) = \pi/2 \), not \( 0 \).
This angle does not even lie in the locked range \( (0, \pi) \), which contains no negative numbers.
This is the value of \( \cot^{-1}(1) \), a completely different input, not \( \cot^{-1}(0) \).

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value of \( \sec^{-1}(1) \)?
questions.explanation:
Since \( \sec(0) = \dfrac{1}{\cos 0} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1 \), and \( 0 \) lies in the locked range \( [0, \pi] \setminus \{\pi/2\} \), the principal value of \( \sec^{-1}(1) \) is \( 0 \).

This is the boundary of the domain \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1,1) \), so it's worth checking explicitly rather than assuming a pattern.
questions.hint: Test the smallest boundary value first: what angle in \( [0,\pi] \) has secant exactly equal to \( 1 \)?
distractor_logic: This is the value EXCLUDED from the range of \( \sec^{-1}x \); it can never be the output at all, let alone at \( x = 1 \).
This is \( \sec^{-1}(-1) \), not \( \sec^{-1}(1) \); the sign of the input was flipped.
Confuses inverse trigonometric functions with identity functions; \( \sec^{-1}x \) does not simply return the input value.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: What is the principal value of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-1) \)?
questions.explanation:
Since \( \operatorname{cosec}\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1 \), and \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) lies in the locked range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \setminus \{0\} \), the principal value of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-1) \) is \( -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

This is the left boundary of both the domain and the range, so it's a natural edge case to check explicitly.
questions.hint: This is the left-boundary counterpart of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(1) = \pi/2 \) — use the odd-function identity to confirm the sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign carried over from the input; this is \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(1) \), not \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-1) \).
This is the single value excluded from the range of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \); it can never be the output for any input, let alone \( x = -1 \).
This angle does not lie in the locked range \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \) at all.

questions.topic: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
questions.question: Which of the following inputs makes \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) undefined?
questions.explanation:
The domain of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), so only inputs strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \) are excluded.

Since \( x = \dfrac12 \) satisfies \( -1 < \dfrac12 < 1 \), it falls inside the excluded open interval, making \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) undefined.
questions.hint: Check each value against the open interval \( (-1,1) \) — anything strictly between \( -1 \) and \( 1 \) is off-limits here.
distractor_logic: \( x = -3 \) lies in \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1, 1) \), the actual domain of \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \), so it is a valid, defined input.
\( x = \sqrt2 \approx 1.41 \) lies outside \( (-1, 1) \), so it is also a valid, defined input.
\( x = -1 \) is a domain boundary point that IS included (giving \( -\pi/2 \)), not excluded.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: The equations \( \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac12 \) and \( \sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac12 \) both hold. What does this pair of equal outputs illustrate about the need to restrict the domain of \( \sin x \)?
options: It shows that \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) has two correct answers, \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \), and either may be used.
It shows an inconsistency in the definition of sine that mathematicians have not yet resolved.

It shows \( \sin x \) is many-one over \( \mathbb{R} \): two different angles give the same output, so without restricting to a branch like \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \), \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) would not have a single well-defined value.
It shows that \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) are actually the same angle written two different ways.
questions.explanation:
This pair of equal sine values is a concrete example of \( \sin x \) being many-one: two distinct angles map to the same output \( \dfrac12 \).

If \( \sin^{-1} \) were defined without restricting the domain first, it would have to return both \( \pi/6 \) and \( 5\pi/6 \) for the input \( \dfrac12 \) — which isn't allowed for a function. Restricting to \( \left[-\pi/2, \pi/2\right] \) keeps only \( \pi/6 \), fixing the problem.
questions.hint: A function needs exactly one output per input — find which of the two given angles survives once the domain is cut down to \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \).
distractor_logic: This is exactly the trap the restriction avoids: a function must return exactly one value, so once the branch \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \) is locked in, only \( \pi/6 \) qualifies as the principal value.
There is no unresolved inconsistency; restricting the domain is the standard, settled way mathematicians make \( \sin x \) invertible.
\( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) and \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) are genuinely different angles (30° and 150°) that simply happen to share the same sine value.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: The graphs of \( y = \tan^{-1}x \) and \( y = \cot^{-1}x \) intersect at exactly one point. What are its coordinates?
questions.explanation:
At an intersection, \( \tan^{-1}x = \cot^{-1}x \). Using \( \tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), substituting gives \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \tan^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), meaning \( x = 1 \).

The single intersection point is \( \left(1, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \); since \( \tan^{-1}x \) is strictly increasing and \( \cot^{-1}x \) is strictly decreasing, this is the only crossing possible.
questions.hint: Set the two expressions equal and use \( \tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \pi/2 \) to pin down \( x \).
distractor_logic: At \( x = 0 \), \( \tan^{-1}(0) = 0 \) but \( \cot^{-1}(0) = \pi/2 \); these values don't match.
At \( x = \sqrt3 \), \( \tan^{-1}(\sqrt3) = \pi/3 \) but \( \cot^{-1}(\sqrt3) = \pi/6 \); these values don't match.
At \( x = -1 \), \( \tan^{-1}(-1) = -\pi/4 \) but \( \cot^{-1}(-1) = 3\pi/4 \); these values don't match — the \( y \)-coordinate here is wrong.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: For \( x \in (0, 1] \), how do the graphs of \( y = \sin^{-1}x \) and \( y = \tan^{-1}x \) compare, and where (if anywhere) do they meet on this interval?
options: \( \sin^{-1}x > \tan^{-1}x \) for every \( x \) in \( (0, 1] \); the two graphs do not meet anywhere on this open-closed interval, only at \( x=0 \) itself.
They meet at \( x = \dfrac12 \), where both equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
They meet at \( x = 1 \), where both equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.explanation:
Both functions are \( 0 \) at \( x=0 \) and increase together, but sine's inverse climbs faster: e.g. at \( x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \), \( \sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785 \), while \( \tan^{-1}x \approx 0.615 \).

Since both are strictly increasing and odd, and \( \sin^{-1}x \) stays above \( \tan^{-1}x \) throughout \( (0,1] \), the two curves touch only at the single shared point \( x = 0 \) and never again on this interval.
questions.hint: Compare the two functions at one convenient test point like \( x = 1/\sqrt2 \) rather than trying to solve an equation directly.
distractor_logic: Checking \( x = \dfrac12 \): \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.524 \) while \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \approx 0.464 \) — sine-inverse is actually the larger one, the opposite of this claim.

At \( x = \dfrac12 \), \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \approx 0.464 \) is NOT equal to \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.524 \); only \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \) equals \( \pi/6 \), not \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) \).
At \( x = 1 \), \( \sin^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), not \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \); only \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \pi/4 \), so the two values disagree here.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: Which of the following correctly identifies a point of symmetry shared by the graphs of \( y = \cos^{-1}x \), \( y = \cot^{-1}x \), and \( y = \sec^{-1}x \)?
options: All three graphs have point symmetry about the origin \( (0, 0) \), since each is an odd function.
All three graphs have point symmetry about \( \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \), since each satisfies \( f(-x) = \pi - f(x) \).
All three graphs are symmetric about the vertical line \( x = 0 \) (a mirror image, not a rotational symmetry).
Only \( \cos^{-1}x \) has this symmetry; \( \cot^{-1}x \) and \( \sec^{-1}x \) do not share it.
questions.explanation:
Each of \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \), \( \cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1}x \), and \( \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x \) is one of the locked complement-type identities from Section 3.

Geometrically, \( f(-x) = \pi - f(x) \) means that rotating the graph \( 180^\circ \) about the point \( \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) maps the curve back onto itself, so all three graphs share this same point of symmetry.
questions.hint: Translate the algebraic identity \( f(-x)=\pi-f(x) \) into a geometric statement about rotating around a fixed point.
distractor_logic: None of \( \cos^{-1}x \), \( \cot^{-1}x \), \( \sec^{-1}x \) are odd functions; they follow the complement-type rule \( \pi - f(x) \), not the odd rule \( -f(x) \), so origin symmetry is the wrong description.
A mirror image about the line \( x=0 \) would require \( f(-x) = f(x) \) (an even function), which none of these three satisfy either.
All three functions share the identical complement-type rule \( f(-x) = \pi - f(x) \), by the locked negative-argument identities in Section 3, so all three share this point symmetry.

questions.question: The graph of \( y = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is split into two disconnected branches by the excluded domain interval \( (-1, 1) \). What is true of the \( y \)-values on the branch where \( x \ge 1 \)?
options: They range over \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \), since this branch lies below the \( x \)-axis.
They range over \( \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), increasing from \( 0 \) toward \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) as \( x \to \infty \).
They range over \( \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), decreasing from \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) (at \( x=1 \)) toward, but never reaching, \( 0 \) as \( x \to \infty \).
They stay fixed at exactly \( y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) for every \( x \ge 1 \).
questions.explanation:
At \( x = 1 \), \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), the largest value this branch reaches. As \( x \to \infty \), \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \to 0^{+} \), since larger cosecant inputs correspond to angles closer to \( 0 \).

Because \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is a decreasing function, this branch sweeps from \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) down to (but never including) \( 0 \), giving the range \( \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) for \( x \ge 1 \).
questions.hint: Evaluate the two ends of this branch directly — at \( x=1 \) and as \( x \to \infty \) — and remember the function is decreasing.
distractor_logic: The \( x \ge 1 \) branch lies at or above the \( x \)-axis, not below it; the negative-\( y \) branch corresponds instead to \( x \le -1 \).
The direction is reversed: since \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) is a decreasing function of \( x \), larger \( x \) gives SMALLER \( y \), not larger.
The value is only exactly \( \pi/2 \) at the single point \( x = 1 \); for larger \( x \), \( y \) genuinely decreases toward \( 0 \), it does not stay fixed.

questions.topic: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
questions.question: A student claims: "Since \( \sec\,\theta \) and \( \cos\,\theta \) are reciprocals, the graph of \( \sec^{-1}x \) must be the reciprocal of the graph of \( \cos^{-1}x \), i.e. \( \sec^{-1}x = \dfrac{1}{\cos^{-1}x} \)." Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: It is not flawed; \( \sec^{-1}x = \dfrac{1}{\cos^{-1}x} \) is in fact a correct identity used throughout this chapter.
It is flawed only because the domains of \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \cos^{-1}x \) happen to be different, but the formula itself is otherwise correct.
It is flawed because \( \cos^{-1}x \) is never zero, so its reciprocal is never even defined.

Taking the reciprocal of a trig ratio (\( \sec\theta = 1/\cos\theta \)) is not the same operation as taking the reciprocal of an inverse trig function's output; the true relationship is \( \sec^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) \) for \( |x| \ge 1 \), which involves the reciprocal of the INPUT, not of the final angle.
questions.explanation:
The reciprocal relationship between \( \sec\theta \) and \( \cos\theta \) is a statement about the TRIG RATIOS themselves (\( \sec\theta = 1/\cos\theta \)), evaluated at the same angle \( \theta \).

It does not carry over to a reciprocal relationship between the two INVERSE FUNCTIONS' outputs. The correct locked identity instead moves the reciprocal onto the input: \( \sin^{-1}(1/x) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) and its cosine analogue \( \cos^{-1}(1/x) = \sec^{-1}x \), for \( |x| \ge 1 \) — never \( 1/\cos^{-1}x \).
questions.hint: Reciprocal identities in this chapter always move the reciprocal onto the \( x \) inside the function, never wrap around the whole inverse-function output.
distractor_logic: This is precisely the flawed identity the question is asking to be identified as wrong — it does not appear anywhere among the locked identities of Section 3, and no such relation holds.

The domain mismatch is a real consequence but not the core error; even restricting to matching domains, \( 1/\cos^{-1}x \) still would not equal \( \sec^{-1}x \) at any shared value (check \( x=1 \): \( \cos^{-1}(1)=0 \), making \( 1/\cos^{-1}(1) \) undefined, while \( \sec^{-1}(1) = 0 \) is perfectly defined).
While \( \cos^{-1}(1) = 0 \) does make this particular reciprocal undefined at one point, that isolated fact isn't why the general formula is wrong across the rest of the domain.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Is the identity \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) valid at \( x = \dfrac12 \)? Explain what actually goes wrong.
options: No — at \( x = \dfrac12 \), the left side becomes \( \sin^{-1}(2) \), which is not defined at all, since \( 2 \) lies outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s domain \( [-1,1] \); the identity fails completely, not just its domain condition on paper.
Yes — the identity holds for all nonzero \( x \), and \( x = \dfrac12 \) is nonzero, so it applies here without issue.
No — the identity fails only because \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\tfrac12\right) \) gives a slightly different numerical answer than \( \sin^{-1}(2) \), a rounding mismatch.
Yes, but only after first simplifying \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) using the negative-argument identity, since \( 2 > 1 \).
questions.explanation:
Substituting \( x = \dfrac12 \) into the left side gives \( \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1/2}\right) = \sin^{-1}(2) \).

Since \( 2 \notin [-1,1] \), \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) is not defined, so the entire left-hand side of the identity breaks down — this is exactly why the domain condition \( |x|\ge 1 \) is stated alongside the identity in the first place, not as an afterthought.
questions.hint: Substitute the specific value into the left side first, before worrying about matching it to the right side.
distractor_logic: This overstates the identity's scope; the true condition is \( |x| \ge 1 \), not merely \( x \ne 0 \), precisely because the left side can become undefined otherwise, as it does here.
This is not a rounding mismatch — \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) isn't a slightly-off number, it is simply undefined, since \( 2 \) is outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s domain \( [-1,1] \) entirely.

The negative-argument identity relates \( f(-x) \) to \( f(x) \) for arguments already inside the domain; it cannot rescue an argument like \( 2 \) that was never in the domain of \( \sin^{-1} \) to begin with.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Using the negative-argument identity, evaluate \( \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) \).
questions.explanation:
By the identity \( \cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x \), the sum becomes \( \left[\pi - \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\right] + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = \pi \).

This confirms a general pattern: for any valid \( x \), \( \cos^{-1}(-x) + \cos^{-1}(x) = \pi \) always, directly from the negative-argument identity — you don't even need the specific standard values to see this.
questions.hint: Apply the identity symbolically first (before plugging in numbers) and watch the \( \cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt3/2\right) \) terms cancel.
distractor_logic: This would be correct if the two terms cancelled to zero, as they would for an odd function like \( \sin^{-1} \), but \( \cos^{-1} \) instead follows the complement-type rule, so the terms add rather than cancel.
This is the value each individual angle would need to differ from a right angle by, not the actual sum requested.
This matches only the second term, \( \cos^{-1}(\sqrt3/2) = \pi/6 \)... actually this equals neither term; it looks like a distractor value rather than a genuine partial answer.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Starting from \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) \), use the complementary-pair identity with \( \sec^{-1} \) to derive its value, then confirm it matches the known standard value.
questions.explanation:
First recall the standard value \( \sec^{-1}(2) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).

Then apply \( \sec^{-1}x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) with \( x = 2 \): \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \), which indeed matches the standard value from the locked table — confirming the identity is self-consistent.
questions.hint: Look up \( \sec^{-1}(2) \) first, then use the complementary-pair identity to derive \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) \) from it, and compare with what you already know.
distractor_logic: Adds instead of subtracts in the complementary-pair identity, and the resulting angle \( 5\pi/6 \) is outside \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \) anyway, which should have signalled an error.

Uses \( \pi - \sec^{-1}(2) \), the negative-argument rule for \( \sec^{-1} \), instead of the complementary-pair rule \( \pi/2 - \sec^{-1}(2) \); also, this result lies outside \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \)'s range.
Uses \( \sec^{-1}(2) = \pi/6 \), but the actual standard value is \( \sec^{-1}(2) = \pi/3 \); this swaps the sec and cosec standard values for the same input.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Is the complementary-pair identity \( \sec^{-1}x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \) valid at \( x = 0 \)?
options: Yes — the identity holds for all real \( x \), including \( x = 0 \), giving \( \sec^{-1}(0) + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(0) = \pi/2 \).
Yes, but only \( \sec^{-1}(0) \) is defined at this value; \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(0) \) is the one that's undefined.
Yes, but only \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(0) \) is defined at this value; \( \sec^{-1}(0) \) is the one that's undefined.
No — at \( x = 0 \), neither \( \sec^{-1}(0) \) nor \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(0) \) is defined, since \( 0 \) fails the required domain condition \( |x| \ge 1 \) for both functions.
questions.explanation:
Both \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) require \( |x| \ge 1 \) to be defined, since their shared domain is \( \mathbb{R} \setminus (-1,1) \).

Since \( x = 0 \) lies strictly inside the excluded interval \( (-1, 1) \), both sides of the identity are undefined there — the identity simply has nothing to say at \( x = 0 \), rather than producing a wrong numeric answer.
questions.hint: Check the domain condition \( |x|\ge 1 \) first — if it fails, neither side of the identity is even defined.
distractor_logic: Overstates the domain; the identity explicitly requires \( |x| \ge 1 \), and \( x=0 \) fails this for both functions, not just one.
Gets the outcome backwards for \( \sec^{-1} \); \( 0 \) lies strictly inside the excluded interval \( (-1,1) \), so \( \sec^{-1}(0) \) is undefined, not defined.
Gets the outcome backwards for \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \); \( 0 \) lies strictly inside the excluded interval \( (-1,1) \), so \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(0) \) is undefined, not defined.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: A student converts \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) \) to \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) using the reciprocal identity, then claims \( \sec^{-1}(3) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) by pattern-matching with \( \sec^{-1}(2) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \). What is the actual issue?
options: The reciprocal conversion to \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) is valid, but the final numeric step is wrong: \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) is a genuine, different angle from \( \sec^{-1}(2) \) — there's no rule making standard-value results transfer to a different input just because both inputs are integers \( \ge 2 \).
The reciprocal conversion itself is invalid, since \( 3 \) doesn't satisfy the domain condition \( |x| \ge 1 \) for \( \sec^{-1} \).
The reciprocal conversion is valid and so is the final value; \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) genuinely equals \( \pi/3 \), same as \( \sec^{-1}(2) \).
The issue is a sign error: the correct value should be \( -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \), not \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.explanation:
The reciprocal identity \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right) = \sec^{-1}x \) correctly converts \( \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac13\right) \) to \( \sec^{-1}(3) \), since \( |3| \ge 1 \).

But this chapter's locked standard-value table only lists \( \sec^{-1} \) at specific inputs like \( 1, 2, \sqrt2, 2/\sqrt3 \) — not \( 3 \). \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) is a perfectly real, well-defined angle, but it is NOT one of the standard \( \pi \)-fraction angles, and definitely not simply equal to \( \sec^{-1}(2) \).
questions.hint: An identity converting between two forms doesn't guarantee the resulting expression is a standard angle — check whether the new argument is actually in the locked standard-value table.
distractor_logic: \( 3 \) does satisfy \( |x| \ge 1 \), so the reciprocal conversion step itself is perfectly valid; the problem lies entirely in the next step.

This is exactly the invalid pattern-matching being tested — \( \sec^{-1}(3) \) is a genuinely different, non-standard angle, not equal to \( \sec^{-1}(2) = \pi/3 \) just because both are secant-inverse of an integer.

There's no sign issue here at all; the input \( 3 \) is positive and the expected output would also be a positive angle in \( [0,\pi] \) — the real issue is assuming the value equals a different, nearby standard angle.

questions.topic: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
questions.question: Using both the odd identity and the reciprocal identity together, express \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2) \) in terms of \( \sin^{-1} \), and simplify to a single standard angle.
questions.explanation:
First apply the odd identity: \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) \).

Then apply the reciprocal identity to the remaining term: \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(2) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \). Combining both steps gives \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \), which matches the standard value directly from the locked table.
questions.hint: Peel off the negative sign with the odd identity first, then convert the remaining positive-argument term using the reciprocal identity.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign that the odd identity \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-x) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) introduces at the first step.
Skips taking the reciprocal of \( x=2 \) before converting; \( \sin^{-1} \)'s domain is \( [-1,1] \), so \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) isn't even defined.
Correctly keeps the sign but uses the wrong standard value; \( \sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \), not \( -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(1) + \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3) \) by applying the sum formula in two stages.
questions.explanation:
First combine \( \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3) \): since \( xy=6>1 \) with both positive, this needs the \( +\pi \) correction, giving \( \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{-5}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).

Then add the remaining term: \( \dfrac{3\pi}{4} + \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \pi \). This is the classic identity \( \tan^{-1}1+\tan^{-1}2+\tan^{-1}3 = \pi \).
questions.hint: Combine two of the three terms first (the ones needing a correction), simplify to a single angle, then add the last term separately.
distractor_logic: This is only the value of \( \tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3) \) alone; the question asks for all three terms combined, which adds the further \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \pi/4 \).
Undershoots substantially; each of the three angles is already fairly large (close to or above \( \pi/4 \)), so their sum must exceed \( \pi/2 \) by a good margin.
Overshoots; the three angles individually are each less than \( \pi/2 \), so their sum cannot reach as high as \( 2\pi \).

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(-2) + \tan^{-1}(-3) \) using the sum formula with the appropriate correction.
questions.explanation:
Here \( x=-2, y=-3 \), so \( xy = 6 > 1 \) and both are negative, triggering the \( -\pi \) correction.

The raw formula gives \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-2-3}{1-6}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-5}{-5}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Applying the correction: \( \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \pi = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Both angles are negative here, so their sum must land below \( -\pi/2 \) — check that your final answer actually does.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; since both original angles \( \tan^{-1}(-2) \) and \( \tan^{-1}(-3) \) are negative, their sum must be negative too.

This is the raw, uncorrected base-formula value with its sign flipped incorrectly — the actual base-formula output here is \( \tan^{-1}(1)=\pi/4 \), which must then have \( \pi \) SUBTRACTED, not left as is.
Uses only the base formula's raw output without applying the required \( -\pi \) correction for the \( x,y<0 \), \( xy>1 \) case.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Does the tangent-form conversion \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right) \) correctly give the value of \( 2\tan^{-1}(2) \) when \( x=2 \) is substituted directly?
options: No — substituting \( x=2 \) gives \( \tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac43\right) \approx -0.93 \), which does not equal \( 2\tan^{-1}(2) \approx 2.21 \); the tangent-form is only valid for \( -1 < x < 1 \), and \( x=2 \) violates that.
Yes — direct substitution always works for this formula regardless of the value of \( x \), since the algebra used to derive it holds for all real \( x \ne \pm1 \).
No — the formula is undefined at \( x=2 \) because the denominator \( 1-x^2 \) becomes zero there.
Yes, but only after also applying a \( +\pi \) correction identical in form to the one used for the sum formula.
questions.explanation:
The tangent-form identity is only stated (and only guaranteed to hold) for \( -1 < x < 1 \), precisely so that \( 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1}x \) stays inside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range \( \left(-\pi/2, \pi/2\right) \).

At \( x=2 \), \( \theta = \tan^{-1}(2) \approx 1.107 \), so \( 2\theta \approx 2.214 \), which is well outside \( \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \). Substituting into the formula anyway gives \( \tan^{-1}(-4/3)\approx -0.927 \), a completely different (and also range-valid) angle — confirming the formula genuinely breaks outside its stated domain.
questions.hint: Compute both sides independently and compare the actual numbers — don't assume the algebra transfers just because the expression is defined.
distractor_logic: The algebraic derivation is valid for all \( x\ne\pm1 \), but the resulting angle only matches \( 2\tan^{-1}x \) when \( 2\tan^{-1}x \) itself stays inside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range \( \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \), which requires \( -1<x<1 \); outside that, the formula's output is a genuinely different (though still well-defined) angle.
The denominator \( 1-x^2 \) at \( x=2 \) is \( 1-4=-3 \), which is not zero; the formula is perfectly well-defined numerically here — it's just numerically wrong as a value for \( 2\tan^{-1}(2) \).
This chapter's locked double-angle formulas carry no such correction term (unlike the separate sum/difference formulas); no such \( +\pi \) fix is part of the stated tangent-form identity.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Can the tangent-form conversion \( 2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right) \) be used to evaluate \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) \) directly?
options: Yes — direct substitution gives \( \tan^{-1}(2) \), which is the correct value of \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) \).
No — at \( x=1 \), the denominator \( 1-x^2 = 0 \), making the expression \( \dfrac{2x}{1-x^2} \) undefined; the sine-form or cosine-form must be used instead.
Yes — direct substitution gives \( \tan^{-1}(0) = 0 \), which is the correct value of \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) \).
No — the formula does technically produce a number, but that number does not equal \( \pi/2 \), the true value of \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) \).
questions.explanation:
At \( x=1 \), the tangent-form's denominator \( 1-x^2 \) equals \( 1-1=0 \), making \( \dfrac{2x}{1-x^2} \) undefined — this reflects the fact that \( \tan(2\theta) \) itself is undefined when \( 2\theta = \pi/2 \), exactly the case here since \( \theta=\tan^{-1}(1)=\pi/4 \).

The sine-form and cosine-form remain perfectly usable, though: \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) = \sin^{-1}(1) = \cos^{-1}(0) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: Check the denominator of the specific form you're about to use before substituting — a zero denominator signals that form breaks down at that particular \( x \), even though other forms may still work fine.
distractor_logic: \( \tan^{-1}(2) \) is not even a standard \( \pi \)-fraction angle, so it cannot equal \( 2\tan^{-1}(1) = \pi/2 \); more fundamentally, the substitution itself is undefined since \( 1-1^2=0 \) causes division by zero.
Division by zero does not produce \( 0 \); the expression \( \dfrac{2}{0} \) is simply undefined, not equal to any real number.
The formula does not "technically produce a number" here at all — \( \dfrac{2(1)}{1-1^2} = \dfrac{2}{0} \) is a division by zero, undefined outright, not merely a wrong value.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac15\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac18\right) \) by applying the sum formula in two stages.
questions.explanation:
First combine \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac15\right) \): since \( xy = \dfrac{1}{10} < 1 \), the base formula applies directly, giving \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac12+\frac15}{1-\frac{1}{10}}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7/10}{9/10}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{9}\right) \).

Then combine this with the remaining term: \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac79\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac18\right) \), with product \( \dfrac{7}{72} < 1 \), giving \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac79+\frac18}{1-\frac{7}{72}}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{65/72}{65/72}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Combine the first two terms into a single (non-standard) tangent-inverse expression first, then combine that result with the third term.
distractor_logic: This does not match the actual chained computation, which reduces all the way down to exactly \( \pi/4 \), one of the standard angles.
Undershoots; combining all three terms via the formula gives a larger result than this.
Stops after only the first application of the sum formula (combining just the first two terms) instead of continuing to combine the result with the third term.

questions.topic: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
questions.question: Using the previously established results \( \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \) and \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(2) + \tan^{-1}(3) - \tan^{-1}(1) \).
questions.explanation:
Since the sum \( \tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3) \) is already known to equal \( \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \), and \( \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), the expression becomes simple arithmetic on angles: \( \dfrac{3\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).

This shows how previously derived results can be reused directly, without re-expanding everything through the formula again from scratch.
questions.hint: You don't need to re-derive anything — just substitute the two known angle values and do the subtraction.
distractor_logic: This ignores the subtraction entirely, as if only \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) were being evaluated on its own.
This adds \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) instead of subtracting it — reversing the sign of the last term.
This is the value of \( \tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3) \) alone, before the subtraction of \( \tan^{-1}(1) \) is applied at all.

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: For \( -1 < x < 1 \), simplify \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\right) \) by substituting \( x = \sin\theta \).
options: \( \theta, \text{ left in terms of the substitution variable} \)
questions.explanation:
Let \( x = \sin\theta \), with \( \theta \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) so that \( \theta = \sin^{-1}x \). Then \( \sqrt{1-x^2} = \sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta} = \cos\theta \) (positive on this interval).

So the expression becomes \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) = \tan^{-1}(\tan\theta) = \theta \), since \( \theta \) already lies inside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s range too. Substituting back, \( \theta = \sin^{-1}x \).
questions.hint: After substituting \( x=\sin\theta \), simplify the square root using \( \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1 \), then recognize the resulting ratio as \( \tan\theta \).
distractor_logic: Mixes up which inverse function the simplification reduces to; the substitution and the resulting ratio \( \tan\theta \) point to \( \theta = \sin^{-1}x \), not \( \cos^{-1}x \).
Doubles the correct answer without justification; no step in this substitution produces a factor of \( 2 \).
Stops the simplification too early; the whole point of the substitution is to express the final answer back in terms of \( x \), not to leave it as the substitution variable \( \theta \).

questions.topic: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
questions.question: For \( -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \le x \le \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \), simplify \( \sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^2}\right) \) by substituting \( x = \sin\theta \).
options: \( \theta, \text{ left in terms of the substitution variable} \)
questions.explanation:
Let \( x = \sin\theta \), with \( \theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right] \) (the range forced by \( -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\le x\le\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \)), so \( \theta = \sin^{-1}x \). Then \( \sqrt{1-x^2} = \cos\theta \).

So the expression becomes \( \sin^{-1}\left(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\right) = \sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta) = 2\theta \), since the restricted range keeps \( 2\theta \in \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \), inside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range. Substituting back, \( 2\theta = 2\sin^{-1}x \).
questions.hint: Recognize \( 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \) as the double-angle identity \( \sin 2\theta \) before applying \( \sin^{-1} \) to it.

topics.name: Definitions, Domain and Principal Value Branches
topics.summary: Before \( \sin^{-1}x \), \( \cos^{-1}x \), and the other four inverse trigonometric functions can be defined, each underlying trig function must first be restricted to a branch on which it is one-one, since a function only has an inverse if each output comes from exactly one input. This branch is called the principal-value branch, and it is locked by convention: \( \sin^{-1} \) uses \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \), \( \cos^{-1} \) uses \( [0,\pi] \), \( \tan^{-1} \) uses \( \left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right) \), \( \cot^{-1} \) uses \( (0,\pi) \), \( \sec^{-1} \) uses \( [0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\} \), and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \) uses \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right]\setminus\{0\} \). The domain of each inverse function is exactly the set of values its underlying trig ratio can actually produce: \( [-1,1] \) for sine and cosine, all of \( \mathbb{R} \) for tangent and cotangent, and \( \mathbb{R}\setminus(-1,1) \) for secant and cosecant. Inputs outside these domains are simply undefined.
topics.worked_example:
Evaluate \( \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) \).

First check the domain: \( -\dfrac12 \in [-1,1] \), so the expression is defined.

The angle in \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \) whose sine is \( -\dfrac12 \) is \( -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \), so \( \sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
common_mistakes: Evaluating \( \cot^{-1}(0) \) as \( 0 \) instead of \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), by mixing up the locked \( (0,\pi) \) branch with a calculator's different default convention.
Assuming an inverse trig function accepts every real number as input, without checking the actual domain (e.g. treating \( \sin^{-1}(2) \) or \( \sec^{-1}(0.5) \) as though they were defined).
Confusing \( \sin^{-1}x \) with the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \), i.e. \( (\sin x)^{-1} \) — these are entirely different expressions.

topics.name: Graphs and Domain–Range Restrictions of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
topics.summary: The graph of each inverse trigonometric function reflects the domain and range locked in its principal-value branch. \( \sin^{-1}x \), \( \tan^{-1}x \), and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) are odd functions, with graphs symmetric about the origin, satisfying \( f(-x)=-f(x) \); \( \cos^{-1}x \), \( \cot^{-1}x \), and \( \sec^{-1}x \) instead share point symmetry about \( \left(0,\pi/2\right) \), satisfying \( f(-x)=\pi-f(x) \). \( \sin^{-1}x \) and \( \tan^{-1}x \) are strictly increasing, while \( \cos^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \) are strictly decreasing. \( \tan^{-1}x \) and \( \cot^{-1}x \) have horizontal asymptotes (at \( \pm\pi/2 \), and at \( 0 \) and \( \pi \), respectively) since their domain is all of \( \mathbb{R} \) with no vertical breaks. \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \), by contrast, have domains with a whole interval, \( (-1,1) \), removed, so their graphs split into two disconnected branches.
key_formulas: \( \tan^{-1}x \) has horizontal asymptotes \( y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \); \( \cot^{-1}x \) has horizontal asymptotes \( y=0 \) and \( y=\pi \)
topics.worked_example:
Find the single point where the graphs of \( y=\sin^{-1}x \) and \( y=\cos^{-1}x \) intersect.

At an intersection, \( \sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}x \). Using \( \sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \), substituting gives \( 2\sin^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \), so \( \sin^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \), meaning \( x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).

The intersection point is \( \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \).
common_mistakes: Assuming \( \cot^{-1}x \) is an odd function like \( \tan^{-1}x \), when it actually follows the \( \pi-\theta \) pattern shared with \( \cos^{-1}x \) and \( \sec^{-1}x \).
Treating the range endpoints \( \pm\pi/2 \) of \( \tan^{-1}x \) as attainable values, rather than as asymptotes the graph only approaches.
Forgetting that \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) have disconnected two-branch graphs, since their domain excludes the whole interval \( (-1,1) \), not just a single point.

topics.name: Property Set 1 — Reciprocal, Negative-Argument and Complementary-Pair Identities
topics.summary: Three families of identities connect the six inverse trigonometric functions without needing full evaluation. Reciprocal identities relate a function to its "co" partner by inverting the argument, always with a domain condition attached, e.g. \( \sin^{-1}\left(1/x\right)=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) for \( |x|\ge1 \). Negative-argument identities describe how each function responds to \( -x \): the odd-symmetric trio (\( \sin^{-1},\tan^{-1},\operatorname{cosec}^{-1} \)) simply flip sign, while the complement-type trio (\( \cos^{-1},\cot^{-1},\sec^{-1} \)) instead give \( \pi \) minus the original value. Complementary-pair identities state that \( \sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x \), \( \tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x \), and \( \sec^{-1}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) each always equal \( \dfrac{\pi}{2} \), on their respective shared domains. Every domain condition attached to these identities is essential — applying an identity outside its stated domain produces an undefined or meaningless expression, not just a "technically wrong" one.
topics.worked_example:
Evaluate \( \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) \) using the negative-argument identity.

\( \cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x \), so \( \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\pi-\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \).
common_mistakes: Dropping the domain condition on a reciprocal identity, e.g. writing \( \sin^{-1}(1/x)=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x \) as though it held for every \( x\ne0 \), instead of only \( |x|\ge1 \).
Over-generalizing the odd-function negative-argument rule to \( \cos^{-1},\cot^{-1} \), or \( \sec^{-1} \), which actually follow the \( \pi-\theta \) rule instead.
Using the wrong condition for the \( \tan^{-1}/\cot^{-1} \) reciprocal identity, which needs \( x>0 \) specifically, unlike the \( |x|\ge1 \) condition on the sine/cosine reciprocal pairs.

topics.name: Property Set 2 — Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Conversion Formulas
topics.summary: The sum and difference formulas convert \( \tan^{-1}x\pm\tan^{-1}y \) into a single \( \tan^{-1} \) expression, mirroring the ordinary tangent addition and subtraction formulas. The sum formula's base form, \( \tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\right) \), only applies directly when \( xy<1 \); once \( xy>1 \), the denominator flips sign and a correction of \( +\pi \) (when both \( x,y>0 \)) or \( -\pi \) (when both \( x,y<0 \)) must be added to recover the true sum. The double-angle conversion formulas rewrite \( 2\tan^{-1}x \) as a single \( \sin^{-1} \), \( \cos^{-1} \), or \( \tan^{-1} \) expression in terms of \( x \) alone, derived from the ordinary double-angle formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent. The tangent-form specifically requires \( -1<x<1 \), since outside that range \( 2\tan^{-1}x \) falls outside \( \tan^{-1} \)'s own range, and the formula breaks down (or, at \( x=\pm1 \), the denominator itself becomes zero).
key_formulas: \( \tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right) \), for \( xy<1 \); add \( \pi \) (if \( x,y>0 \)) or subtract \( \pi \) (if \( x,y<0 \)) when \( xy>1 \)
topics.worked_example:
Evaluate \( \tan^{-1}(2)+\tan^{-1}(3) \).

Since \( xy=6>1 \) and both \( x,y>0 \), the \( +\pi \) correction is required.

The raw formula gives \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2+3}{1-6}\right)=\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\dfrac{\pi}{4} \). Adding the correction: \( \pi+\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the \( \pm\pi \) quadrant correction whenever \( xy>1 \), and reporting the raw (wrong-branch) base-formula output as the final answer.
Applying the tangent-form double-angle conversion at a value like \( x=2 \) or \( x=1 \), outside the required \( -1<x<1 \), where the formula either gives a wrong-branch value or divides by zero.
Mixing up the direction of the correction — adding \( \pi \) when both values are negative (should subtract), or vice versa.

topics.name: Simplification and Evaluation of Composite Inverse Trigonometric Expressions
topics.summary: Composite expressions combine an inverse trigonometric function with an ordinary trigonometric function, in either order, and the two orders behave very differently. Going "trig of inverse-trig", such as \( \sin(\sin^{-1}x) \), always simplifies directly to \( x \) for any \( x \) in the domain, with no range check needed. Going "inverse-trig of trig", such as \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) \), only simplifies directly to \( \theta \) when \( \theta \) already lies inside the relevant principal-value range; otherwise, \( \theta \) must first be replaced with the equivalent angle, inside that range, that shares the same trig ratio. Composite expressions mixing two different trig functions, such as \( \sin(\cos^{-1}x) \), are simplified algebraically using the Pythagorean relation \( \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1 \) together with a sign check based on which quadrant the intermediate angle's range restricts it to.
key_formulas: \( f(f^{-1}(x))=x \) always, for \( x \) in the domain of \( f^{-1} \) (no range check needed)
\( f^{-1}(f(\theta))=\theta \) only when \( \theta \) already lies inside \( f^{-1} \)'s principal-value range; otherwise reduce \( \theta \) to its in-range equivalent first
\( \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1 \), used with a quadrant/sign check based on the intermediate angle's known range, to simplify mixed composite expressions
topics.worked_example:
Evaluate \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \).

Since \( \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \) lies outside \( \sin^{-1} \)'s range \( \left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right] \), it must be replaced by an in-range angle with the same sine.

Using \( \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\sin\left(\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \), and since \( \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) IS inside the range, \( \sin^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
common_mistakes: Assuming \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)=\theta \) (or the analogous rule for any of the six functions) always holds, without first checking whether \( \theta \) lies inside the principal-value range.
Dropping the sign of a Pythagorean-relation term (e.g. writing \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \) as negative) without checking which quadrant the intermediate angle's range actually restricts it to.
Confusing the two composition orders — treating \( \sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) \) as though it needed no range check, the way \( \sin(\sin^{-1}x) \) does.
